scenes.heading: Cell theory and cell types
scenes.sub: Why every living thing is built from tiny cells
scenes.say: From a bacterium in yoghurt, to a gum tree, to you, every living thing is made of cells. But why are cells so small, and how do you tell the types apart?

scenes.heading: Cell theory
points: All living things are made of cells
The cell is the basic unit of life
All cells come from pre-existing cells
scenes.say: Cell theory has three parts. All living things are made of cells. The cell is the basic unit of life. And all cells come from pre-existing cells, by cell division.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A studio flat is one open room; a house has separate rooms
scenes.science: Prokaryotes have no nucleus; eukaryotes have a nucleus and organelles
scenes.breaks: A studio flat isn't less of a home. Prokaryotes aren't simple leftovers; they are hugely successful cells.
scenes.say: A prokaryotic cell is like a studio flat: everything is in one open space, and its DNA sits in the nucleoid. A eukaryotic cell is like a house with rooms: DNA in the nucleus, and other jobs in membrane-bound organelles. But prokaryotes aren't simple leftovers. They're hugely successful cells.

scenes.heading: Prokaryotic vs eukaryotic
scenes.say: Pro equals no, eu equals do. Prokaryotes, like bacteria, have no nucleus, circular DNA with plasmids, and smaller ribosomes. They're about one to ten micrometres. Eukaryotes have a nucleus, linear DNA in several chromosomes, and are about ten to one hundred micrometres.
scenes.caption: Pro = no, eu = do. Prokaryotes, like bacteria, have no nucleus, circular DNA with plasmids, and smaller ribosomes. They're about 1–10 µm. Eukaryotes have a nucleus, linear DNA in several chromosomes, and are about 10–100 µm.

scenes.heading: Plant cells' three Cs
points: A wall alone doesn't prove it's a plant cell
scenes.say: Plant cells have three Cs that animal cells don't: a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole. But careful! Bacteria and fungi have cell walls too.

scenes.heading: Surface area to volume
scenes.question: Model cells as cubes with sides of 1 cm, 2 cm and 4 cm. Which has the highest SA:V?
lines: Smallest cube has the highest SA:V
scenes.say: Cells swap materials through their membrane, so surface area to volume ratio matters. Model cells as cubes. The one centimetre cube has a ratio of six to one. The two centimetre cube, three to one. The four centimetre cube, one and a half to one. Double the side, halve the ratio. Small cells exchange materials best.
scenes.caption: Cells swap materials through their membrane, so SA:V matters. Model cells as cubes. The 1 cm cube has a ratio of 6 : 1. The 2 cm cube, 3 : 1. The 4 cm cube, 1.5 : 1. Double the side, halve the ratio. Small cells exchange materials best.

scenes.heading: Ways to boost SA:V
points: Be flat or long and thin
scenes.say: To keep the ratio high, cells stay small or divide, become flat like red blood cells, or fold their membrane into microvilli.

points: All cells come from existing cells
scenes.say: Quick recap. All cells come from existing cells. Prokaryotes have no nucleus, eukaryotes do. Plant cells have a cellulose wall, chloroplasts and a central vacuole. And as a cell grows, its surface area to volume ratio falls, which limits cell size. Now try the practice questions!
